turns.t: Come in, sit down. I have the note here from your last visit, and the letter from the hospital about your father. I'm very sorry for your loss.
Thanks. It's been a rough few weeks.
I'm sure it has. You asked for this appointment yourself. What was on your mind when you booked it?
Sleep, mostly. I'm not getting any.
Tell me what the sleep is like. Do you struggle to get off, or do you wake?
I get off grand. Then I'm awake at four in the morning, wide awake, and that's me for the day.
Awake at four and not getting back. How long has that been going on?
Since the funeral. Three weeks, near enough.
Okay. And what happens in your head at four in the morning?
Just going over things. The last week in the hospital. Whether I should have pushed them more.
That's a heavy thing to go over in the dark. Apart from the sleep, how's your mood in general?
Low. I'm feeling low, I suppose.
When did you first notice the low feeling? Was it after your father died, or before it?
I couldn't tell you. It might've been there before, when he was getting worse. I don't know.
That's fair enough, it's hard to separate out. We'll leave the date open and not force it.
Yeah.
I have to ask this of everyone in your position. Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?
No. Never. I've the kids to think of.
Good, I'm glad you told me. Now, your health in general. Anything long-term I should know about?
Asthma. Since I was a child. It's been quiet.
Asthma, quiet at the moment. Good. And family history, what did your father die of, if you don't mind me asking?
Lung cancer. He smoked all his life.
I'm sorry. Anyone else in the family with a serious illness?
My sister had breast cancer. She's well now, thank God.
Glad to hear she's well. What about work and home, who's around you at the moment?
I run the farm with my husband. Two kids at home, they're ten and thirteen.
So you're busy with the farm and the children. And are you leaning on anything to get through the evenings, drink or otherwise?
I'm drinking a bit more in the evenings. A glass of whiskey, maybe two.
Thank you for being straight with me. That's common after a death, but it can make the four a.m. waking worse.
I'd say it does.

Right, let me lay out the options. One, we talk about sleep habits and I give you some practical things to try. Two, I refer you to the bereavement counselling service. Three, we check your bloods in case something physical is adding to it.
What would the bloods be looking for?
Mainly your thyroid and your iron, and a general screen. Tiredness and low mood can have a physical side, and it's easy to rule out.
Do the bloods, then.
I'll order the blood tests for you, and you can have them done at the front desk before you go.
Grand. And the counselling?
I'd recommend it. I'll refer you to the bereavement service, and they'll ring you within a fortnight. Would you be happy to talk to someone?
I'd rather not, but I'll give it a go. Mam says I should.
Your mam sounds sensible. Now, on the sleep. No screens in the last hour, same time to bed every night, and keep the whiskey for the weekend, if at all.
I can try that.
Don't lie in bed fighting it either. If you're awake at four, get up, have a cup of tea in the kitchen and sit with a book, then go back when you're drowsy.
The cows would be glad of the company anyway.
Ha, they would. And I'm not going to put you on tablets today. It's early, and the first thing is to give the other steps a fair try.
That suits me. I don't like tablets.
Understood. I'd like to see you again in three weeks, to see how the sleep is, and to go through the blood results.
Three weeks. I'll have the hay in by then.
Good. If things feel worse before that, ring the surgery and ask for me. Don't wait it out.
I will.
Is there anything you wanted to ask that we haven't covered?
Not really. It's helped to say it out loud.
I'm glad. It often does.
Right so. I'll head and get the bloods.
Go on, mind yourself. See you in three weeks.
Thanks, doctor.
Safe home.
Bye now.
Bye.
